title: Stablecoin Complete Guide
subtitle: Understanding and Using Stablecoins in the Crypto Ecosystem

intro.title: Introduction to Stablecoins
intro.content:
Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a stable value, typically pegged to a fiat currency like the US Dollar. They solve one of crypto's biggest problems: price volatility. While Bitcoin and Ethereum can swing 10-20% in a day, stablecoins aim to stay at exactly $1.00.

This makes them essential infrastructure for the crypto ecosystem. Without stablecoins, you'd need to constantly move between crypto and traditional bank accounts. With stablecoins, you can hold a stable value entirely on-chain, use it in DeFi protocols, send cross-border payments instantly, and earn yield—all without dealing with banks.

As of 2025, stablecoins represent over $200 billion in market cap and process hundreds of billions in monthly transaction volume. Understanding how they work, their differences, and their risks is crucial for anyone in crypto.

stablecoin_types.title: Types of Stablecoins
stablecoin_types.content: Not all stablecoins are created equal. They use fundamentally different mechanisms to maintain their peg, each with unique trade-offs in decentralization, capital efficiency, and stability.

fiat_backed.title: Fiat-Backed Stablecoins
fiat_backed.content:
The simplest and most popular type. For every stablecoin issued, there's $1 (or equivalent) held in a bank account or treasury bonds. This is the traditional IOU model brought to blockchain.

How it works:

  1. User deposits $1 USD with the issuer
  2. Issuer mints 1 stablecoin token on-chain
  3. User can redeem the token for $1 USD anytime

Examples: USDC (Circle), USDT (Tether), BUSD (Binance, deprecated)

Advantages:

  • Simple to understand: 1 token = $1 in bank
  • Strong peg: Backed by actual dollars or equivalents
  • Capital efficient: 1:1 backing ratio
  • Regulatory clarity: Easier to comply with regulations

Disadvantages:

  • Centralized: Issuer can freeze accounts, blacklist addresses
  • Custodial risk: Relies on traditional banking system
  • Transparency concerns: Requires trust in reserve audits
  • Regulatory risk: Subject to government control

crypto_backed.title: Crypto-Collateralized Stablecoins
crypto_backed.content:
Instead of fiat, these stablecoins are backed by other cryptocurrencies. Since crypto is volatile, they require overcollateralization—you deposit $1.50+ of crypto to mint $1 of stablecoin.

How it works (using MakerDAO/DAI as example):

  1. User deposits $150 of ETH as collateral
  2. User borrows/mints up to $100 of DAI (66% LTV ratio)
  3. If ETH drops and collateral ratio falls below minimum, position gets liquidated
  4. To get ETH back, user must repay the DAI plus stability fee (interest)

Examples: DAI (MakerDAO), crvUSD (Curve), sUSD (Synthetix)

Advantages:

  • Decentralized: No central issuer, governed by smart contracts and DAOs
  • Transparent: All collateral visible on-chain
  • Censorship resistant: No one can freeze your assets
  • Composable: Works seamlessly with other DeFi protocols

Disadvantages:

  • Capital inefficient: Need $1.50+ to get $1 stablecoin
  • Complex mechanisms: Requires understanding of CDPs, liquidations, stability fees
  • Liquidation risk: Volatile collateral can trigger cascading liquidations
  • Peg instability: Can trade above/below $1 during market stress

algorithmic.title: Algorithmic Stablecoins
algorithmic.content:
These attempt to maintain the peg through algorithms and incentive mechanisms, often with minimal or no collateral. History has shown this is extremely difficult to execute successfully.

Pure algorithmic (mostly failed):

  • Use supply expansion/contraction to maintain peg
  • Issue bonds or secondary tokens to absorb volatility
  • Major failures: UST/LUNA ($40B collapse), IRON, Basis Cash

Fractional/Hybrid approach (more successful):

FRAX pioneered a fractional-algorithmic model that combines collateral with algorithmic mechanisms:

  • Partially backed by USDC (collateral ratio adjusts based on demand)
  • Partially backed by FXS (protocol token) that is burned/minted
  • Collateral ratio increases during market stress, decreases during stability
  • More capital efficient than fully-backed, more stable than purely algorithmic

Advantages:

  • Capital efficient: Can be under-collateralized or uncollateralized
  • Scalable: Not limited by collateral availability
  • Innovative: Explores new stability mechanisms

Disadvantages:

  • Complex: Hard to understand failure modes
  • Unproven: Most have failed spectacularly
  • Death spiral risk: Loss of confidence can trigger rapid collapse
  • Regulatory uncertainty: May be classified as securities

Important: Pure algorithmic stablecoins have a poor track record. Even sophisticated users lost billions in UST. Approach with extreme caution.

major_stablecoins.title: Major Stablecoins Deep Dive
major_stablecoins.content: Let's examine the leading stablecoins that dominate the market and power most DeFi activity.

usdt.title: USDT (Tether) - The Pioneer
usdt.content:
Launch: 2014
Type: Fiat-backed
Market Cap: ~$120B (largest stablecoin)
Issuer: Tether Limited

Strengths:

  • Liquidity king: Highest trading volume across all exchanges
  • Multi-chain: Available on 15+ blockchains (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, etc.)
  • Battle-tested: 10+ years of operation through multiple market cycles
  • Deep integration: Accepted everywhere in crypto

Controversies:

  • Reserve transparency: Historical lack of clear audits
  • Regulatory scrutiny: Investigations and fines for misleading reserve claims
  • Commercial paper exposure: Previously held significant non-cash reserves

Current status (2025): Tether has improved transparency with regular attestations and shifted reserves to safer assets (primarily US Treasuries). However, it remains more controversial than USDC from a regulatory perspective.

Best for: Maximum liquidity, especially in CEX trading and emerging markets where USDT dominates.

usdc.title: USDC (USD Coin) - The Regulated Choice
usdc.content:
Launch: 2018
Type: Fiat-backed
Market Cap: ~$35B
Issuer: Circle (consortium with Coinbase)

Strengths:

  • Regulatory compliance: Fully regulated in the US
  • Transparency: Monthly attestation reports by top accounting firms
  • Reserve quality: 100% backed by cash and short-duration US Treasuries
  • DeFi integration: Preferred stablecoin for many DeFi protocols
  • Institutional adoption: Used by major financial institutions

Weaknesses:

  • Centralization: Circle can freeze accounts (has done so for sanctioned addresses)
  • Banking dependency: Exposed to traditional banking system risks
  • Lower liquidity: Less trading volume than USDT

March 2023 SVB Crisis: USDC briefly de-pegged to $0.88 when Silicon Valley Bank (holding ~$3.3B of reserves) collapsed. Circle quickly moved reserves and USDC recovered to peg within days. This highlighted centralized stablecoin risks but also showed resilience.

Best for: DeFi protocols, users prioritizing regulatory compliance and transparency, US-based operations.

dai.title: DAI - The Decentralized Standard
dai.content:
Launch: 2017
Type: Crypto-collateralized
Market Cap: ~$5B
Issuer: MakerDAO (decentralized organization)

How DAI works:

  1. Users open Vaults (formerly CDPs) by depositing collateral (ETH, WBTC, stETH, etc.)
  2. Users generate/borrow DAI against their collateral (typically max 66% LTV)
  3. Users pay a Stability Fee (interest rate) set by MKR governance
  4. If collateral value drops too much, the Vault gets liquidated with a penalty
  5. The Peg Stability Module (PSM) allows 1:1 swaps between DAI and USDC for tight peg

Strengths:

  • Decentralized: No company controls it, governed by MKR token holders
  • Transparent: All collateral and operations visible on-chain
  • Censorship resistant: Cannot be frozen or seized
  • Multi-collateral: Accepts diverse crypto assets as collateral
  • DeFi native: Designed for composability with other protocols

Concerns:

  • RWA backing: ~60% of DAI is now backed by Real World Assets (mostly US Treasuries via PSM's USDC). This introduces centralization and regulatory risk.
  • Complexity: Requires active management to avoid liquidation
  • Peg stability: Trades above/below $1 more often than fiat-backed coins

Best for: DeFi users who prioritize decentralization and censorship resistance, willing to accept slightly looser peg.

others.title: Other Notable Stablecoins
others.content:
FRAX - Fractional-Algorithmic Pioneer

  • Hybrid model: Partially collateralized (USDC) + algorithmic (FXS burn/mint)
  • Collateral ratio adjusts based on market conditions (currently ~92%)
  • Innovative stability mechanisms including AMO (Algorithmic Market Operations)
  • Market cap: ~$650M

crvUSD - Curve's Lending Liquidation AMM (LLAMMA)

  • Overcollateralized by crypto assets
  • Revolutionary liquidation mechanism: soft liquidations instead of hard liquidations
  • When collateral price drops, gradually converts to stablecoin; if price recovers, converts back
  • Reduces liquidation risk and losses for borrowers
  • Market cap: ~$150M but growing

sUSD - Synthetix Stablecoin

  • Backed by SNX token (highly overcollateralized, ~400%+ ratio)
  • Part of Synthetix synthetic asset ecosystem
  • Used primarily within Synthetix for trading synthetic assets

TUSD, USDP, GUSD - Other Fiat-Backed Options

  • Similar to USDC but smaller market caps
  • TUSD (TrueUSD): ~$500M
  • USDP (Pax Dollar): ~$400M
  • GUSD (Gemini Dollar): ~$350M

use_cases.title: Stablecoin Use Cases
use_cases.content: Stablecoins aren't just a store of value—they're active infrastructure that enables new financial activities. Here are the main ways people use stablecoins.

trading.title: Trading and Portfolio Management
trading.content:
The original use case: taking profits without leaving crypto.

Traditional approach:

  1. Crypto pumps, you want to lock in profits
  2. Sell to exchange, withdraw to bank account (1-5 days, fees apply)
  3. Want to buy back in? Deposit to exchange (another 1-5 days, more fees)
  4. Miss the opportunity

Stablecoin approach:

  1. Swap ETH for USDC in 12 seconds on-chain
  2. Profits secured at stable value
  3. Market dips? Swap back to ETH instantly
  4. Total time: minutes, not days

Portfolio rebalancing: Professional traders use stablecoins as the hub of their portfolio. Instead of trading BTC→ETH directly, trade BTC→USDC→ETH. This gives better prices on liquid pairs and clearer accounting.

Risk management: When market looks unstable, shift portfolio to stablecoins. Earn yield on your stablecoins (3-8% APY) while waiting for entry opportunities.

defi.title: DeFi Protocols and Yield Generation
defi.content:
Stablecoins are the foundation of DeFi. Most yield opportunities involve stablecoins because they offer returns without price volatility risk.

Lending markets:

  • Supply USDC to Aave: earn 3-6% APY from borrowers
  • Supply DAI to Compound: earn interest + COMP rewards
  • Lower risk than lending volatile assets like ETH

Liquidity provision:

  • Curve 3pool (DAI/USDC/USDT): earn trading fees with minimal impermanent loss
  • Stablecoin pairs have negligible IL since prices move together
  • Combined APY: 4-12% depending on pool and incentives

Leverage and delta-neutral strategies:

  • Borrow stablecoins against ETH collateral, farm with the stables, keep ETH exposure
  • Take out DAI loan at 3% interest, earn 8% on Curve, profit 5% spread
  • Advanced: recursive lending (deposit → borrow → deposit → borrow...)

Cross-chain DeFi: Bridge stablecoins to L2s (Arbitrum, Optimism) or alt-L1s (Solana, Avalanche) for higher yields and lower fees.

payments.title: Payments and Commerce
payments.content:
Stablecoins are becoming a serious alternative to traditional payment rails, especially for online and international commerce.

Merchant adoption:

  • Accept USDC/USDT without volatility risk
  • Settlement in seconds vs 2-3 days for credit cards
  • Lower fees than card processing (2.9% + $0.30)
  • No chargebacks (merchants take fraud risk, but also no false disputes)

Payroll and contractor payments:

  • Pay global contractors in USDC—they receive it instantly
  • No bank intermediaries, no SWIFT delays
  • Popular in crypto companies and remote-first organizations

B2B settlements:

  • Large businesses using stablecoins for supplier payments
  • Especially valuable for cross-border B2B transactions
  • Example: Asian manufacturer paid in USDC by US retailer, settles in minutes

Current limitations: Regulatory uncertainty, accounting complexity, limited consumer adoption (most people still prefer credit cards for protection).

remittance.title: Remittances and Cross-Border Transfers
remittance.content:
Perhaps stablecoins' most compelling real-world use case. Traditional remittance is broken—it's slow, expensive, and excludes billions.

Traditional remittance problems:

  • Expensive: Average fee 6-7% (World Bank data)
  • Slow: 3-5 days for international transfers
  • Limited access: Requires bank accounts on both ends
  • Opaque: Hidden fees in FX conversion

Stablecoin remittance:

  • Near-zero fees: $0.50-$5 regardless of amount (blockchain gas fee)
  • Instant: Settlement in seconds to minutes
  • Open access: Just need internet and wallet
  • Transparent: See exact amount received

Real-world adoption:

  • Latin America: Major growth in USDT usage for remittances and savings
  • Africa: Stablecoins bypassing weak local currencies and expensive money transfer services
  • Southeast Asia: Workers sending money home via stablecoins to avoid 10%+ fees

Challenges: Last-mile conversion to local currency, regulatory clarity, user education, wallet security.

Impact: A worker sending $200 home monthly saves ~$840/year by using stablecoins instead of Western Union. For families living on <$10/day, this is life-changing.

yield_opportunities.title: Earning Yield with Stablecoins
yield_opportunities.content: One of stablecoins' biggest advantages: earn returns without price volatility. Traditional savings accounts pay near-zero interest. DeFi stablecoin yields range from 3-15%+ APY.

lending.title: Lending Protocols
lending.content:
The safest and simplest way to earn on stablecoins: supply them to lending protocols and earn interest from borrowers.

How it works:

  1. Deposit USDC/DAI/USDT into Aave or Compound
  2. Receive interest-bearing tokens (aUSDC, cDAI, etc.)
  3. Interest accrues automatically every block (~12 seconds)
  4. Withdraw anytime (except if 100% utilization—rare)

Current rates (typical ranges, vary by market):

  • Aave: 2-7% APY on USDC/USDT/DAI
  • Compound: 2-6% APY + COMP rewards
  • Higher during volatility: When traders need leverage, borrow demand spikes, rates increase

Risk factors:

  • Smart contract risk: Protocol gets hacked (mitigated by audits, insurance, time-tested code)
  • Utilization risk: If 100% borrowed, can't withdraw until someone repays (very rare)
  • Rate volatility: APY fluctuates based on supply/demand

Pro tip: Use aggregators like Yearn Finance to automatically move funds to highest-yield opportunities and auto-compound.

liquidity_pools.title: Liquidity Pools and AMMs
liquidity_pools.content:
Earn trading fees by providing liquidity to decentralized exchanges. For stablecoin pools, this is low risk with steady returns.

Curve Finance - The Stablecoin LP King:

Curve specializes in stablecoin swaps with minimal slippage. Major pools:

  • 3pool (DAI/USDC/USDT): The most liquid stablecoin pool in DeFi
  • Base APY: 1-4% from trading fees
  • Boosted APY: 3-10%+ with CRV rewards and veCRV boost
  • Additional yield: Stake LP tokens in Convex for boosted CRV rewards

Why Curve for stablecoins?

  • Specialized algorithm for assets with similar prices (low slippage)
  • Minimal impermanent loss (stablecoins stay ~$1)
  • Deep liquidity attracts high volume = more fees

Uniswap V3 Stablecoin Ranges:

  • Concentrate liquidity in tight range (e.g., $0.995-$1.005)
  • Much higher capital efficiency than V2
  • Earn higher fees per dollar, but requires active management
  • Risk: If stablecoin depegs outside your range, you stop earning

Returns breakdown:

  • Conservative (Aave/Compound): 3-6% APY, minimal management
  • Moderate (Curve 3pool): 5-10% APY, stake and forget
  • Active (Curve + Convex): 8-15% APY, claim and compound regularly
  • Advanced (Uniswap V3): 10-20%+ APY, requires active rebalancing

Risk note: Higher yields often mean higher risks or more active management. Start with battle-tested protocols like Aave and Curve.

risks.title: Stablecoin Risks and Safety
risks.content: Stablecoins are called "stable" but they're not risk-free. Understanding the risks is essential for protecting your capital.

depeg_risk.title: De-peg Risk
depeg_risk.content:
When a stablecoin's price deviates from its $1.00 peg. This can range from small fluctuations (±0.5%) to catastrophic collapse (→$0).

Historical de-peg events:

  • UST/LUNA (May 2022): $1.00 → $0.00 in 72 hours. $40B+ in value destroyed. Death spiral: UST lost peg → LUNA minted to restore peg → LUNA hyperinflation → both collapsed.
  • USDC (March 2023): $1.00 → $0.88 when SVB collapsed holding $3.3B reserves. Recovered to $1.00 within days after Circle moved reserves.
  • DAI (March 2020): Briefly traded at $1.05-$1.12 during Black Thursday liquidation cascade. MakerDAO added USDC to PSM to strengthen peg.

Why de-pegs happen:

  • Fiat-backed: Reserve concerns, banking issues, regulatory actions
  • Crypto-backed: Collateral volatility, liquidation cascades, smart contract bugs
  • Algorithmic: Death spirals, loss of confidence, arbitrage mechanisms breaking

Protection strategies:

  • Diversify: Don't hold 100% in one stablecoin
  • Monitor: Watch for price deviation from $1 on aggregators
  • Know your exits: Have plan for where to swap if de-peg occurs
  • Prefer proven: USDC/USDT/DAI have recovered from issues; new stables are untested

regulatory.title: Regulatory Risk
regulatory.content:
Stablecoins sit at the intersection of crypto and traditional finance, making them prime targets for regulation.

Key regulatory concerns:

  • Banking laws: Are stablecoin issuers banks? Do they need banking licenses?
  • Securities classification: Are stablecoins securities subject to SEC oversight?
  • AML/KYC: Requirements for Know Your Customer and anti-money laundering
  • Reserve requirements: What must back stablecoins? How often must it be audited?

Potential regulatory actions:

  • Issuer restrictions: Only licensed entities can issue stablecoins
  • Delisting: Exchanges forced to delist non-compliant stablecoins
  • Capital controls: Limits on stablecoin usage for cross-border payments
  • Forced redemptions: Requirements to redeem at par that issuers can't meet

Geographic differences:

  • US: Increasing scrutiny, likely stablecoin legislation in 2025-2026
  • EU: MiCA (Markets in Crypto-Assets) regulation taking effect 2024-2025
  • Asia: Mixed—Singapore embracing, China banning, Japan regulating

What this means for users:

  • Expect more KYC requirements to buy/sell stablecoins
  • Smaller/unregulated stablecoins may be delisted
  • Increased transparency is good, but also more centralized control

centralization.title: Centralization Risk
centralization.content:
Most stablecoins have central points of control that can freeze, seize, or censor transactions. This is the trade-off for regulatory compliance and fiat backing.

USDC/USDT freeze powers:

  • Circle (USDC) and Tether (USDT) can blacklist addresses
  • Once blacklisted, those tokens are frozen forever
  • This is required to comply with law enforcement requests
  • Real cases: Tornado Cash addresses blacklisted, sanctioned entities blocked

Centralized failure modes:

  • Banking access: If Circle/Tether lose banking partners, issuance/redemption stops
  • Government seizure: Reserves could be frozen by authorities
  • Company failure: If issuer goes bankrupt, recovery uncertain

DAI's centralization paradox:

  • DAI is "decentralized" but ~60% backed by USDC (centralized stablecoin)
  • If USDC fails, DAI is heavily impacted
  • MakerDAO's endgame plan aims to reduce RWA dependency

Mitigation:

  • Know the trade-offs: Fiat-backed = centralized but stable; crypto-backed = decentralized but complex
  • Diversify: Hold mix of centralized (USDC) and decentralized (DAI) stables
  • Accept reality: Complete decentralization with perfect peg stability doesn't exist yet

smart_contract.title: Smart Contract Risk
smart_contract.content:
For crypto-collateralized and algorithmic stablecoins, smart contract bugs can lead to catastrophic losses.

Historical hacks/bugs:

  • bZx (2020): Flash loan attack exploited oracle manipulation, affected stablecoin collateral
  • Mango Markets (2022): Oracle manipulation drained $100M+, affected stablecoin pools
  • Euler Finance (2023): $200M+ hack affected multiple stablecoins in lending pools (funds later returned)

Risk factors:

  • Code complexity: More complex = more attack surface (Curve LLAMMA is innovative but complex)
  • Oracle dependencies: Price feed manipulation can cause incorrect liquidations
  • Composability risk: Bug in one protocol can cascade to others
  • Upgrade risks: Protocol upgrades can introduce vulnerabilities

Due diligence checklist:

  • Audits: Has the protocol been audited? By whom? (Trail of Bits, OpenZeppelin, etc.)
  • Time-tested: How long has code been in production without issues?
  • Bug bounties: Does the protocol offer rewards for finding vulnerabilities?
  • Insurance: Can you buy smart contract insurance? (Nexus Mutual, InsurAce)
  • TVL: Higher TVL often means more scrutiny and white-hat attention

Best practices:

  • Don't ape into new stablecoin protocols
  • Start with small amounts to test
  • Diversify across multiple protocols
  • Consider insurance for large positions

tracking_tools.title: Monitoring and Tracking Tools
tracking_tools.content:
Stay informed about stablecoin health, yields, and market dynamics with these essential tools:

DefiLlama - Comprehensive DeFi Analytics:

  • Track total stablecoin market caps and dominance
  • Monitor TVL across all protocols
  • Compare yields across lending platforms
  • View stablecoin flow between chains
  • Charts showing stablecoin supply changes over time

Curve Analytics - Stablecoin Trading Data:

  • Real-time stablecoin prices and pool balances
  • Trading volume and fee generation for stablecoin pools
  • Identify de-peg events early (when pool imbalances occur)
  • Monitor LP yields and CRV emissions

CoinGecko/CoinMarketCap:

  • Price tracking for all major stablecoins
  • Quick way to spot de-pegs (price ≠ $1.00)
  • Market cap rankings and 24h volume
  • Historical price charts

Attestation and Reserve Reports:

  • USDC: circle.com/en/usdc (monthly attestations by Grant Thornton)
  • USDT: tether.to/en/transparency (quarterly reserve reports)
  • DAI: daistats.com (real-time on-chain collateral data)

On-chain Analytics:

  • Dune Analytics: Custom dashboards for stablecoin metrics
  • Nansen: Whale wallet tracking, smart money flows
  • Etherscan: Verify smart contract code and token holders

What to monitor:

  • Price: Should stay at $1.00 ±0.5%
  • Market cap: Rapid decreases may signal loss of confidence
  • Trading volume: Spikes can indicate panic selling
  • Reserves: For fiat-backed, ensure full backing
  • Collateral ratio: For crypto-backed, watch for under-collateralization

Set up alerts: Use CoinGecko price alerts or Dune dashboard notifications to get notified if your stablecoin deviates from peg.

stablecoin.definition: A cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value, typically pegged to a fiat currency like USD. Enables stable value storage and transactions within the crypto ecosystem.

peg.definition: The target price that a stablecoin aims to maintain, usually $1.00 USD. A strong peg means the stablecoin consistently trades at or very near $1.00.

depeg.definition: When a stablecoin's market price deviates significantly from its intended peg (e.g., trading at $0.95 or $1.05 instead of $1.00). Can range from temporary fluctuations to permanent collapse.

collateral_ratio.definition: The ratio of collateral value to stablecoin debt. For example, a 150% collateral ratio means $1.50 of collateral backs $1.00 of stablecoin. Higher ratios provide more safety buffer.

overcollateralized.definition: When collateral value exceeds debt value. Crypto-backed stablecoins require overcollateralization (e.g., 150%) due to crypto volatility. Provides safety margin for price drops.

algorithmic_stablecoin.definition: A stablecoin that uses algorithms and incentive mechanisms to maintain its peg, often with minimal or no collateral. Most pure algorithmic stablecoins have failed (UST, IRON, etc.).

fiat_backed.definition: Stablecoins backed 1:1 by fiat currency (USD) or equivalents held in reserve. Each token is redeemable for $1. Examples: USDC, USDT. Centralized but simple and capital efficient.

cdp.definition: A smart contract where users lock collateral and generate (borrow) stablecoins. Used by MakerDAO for DAI creation. Also called "Vaults" in current MakerDAO terminology.

psm.definition: A MakerDAO mechanism allowing 1:1 swaps between DAI and other stablecoins (mainly USDC) with near-zero fees. Helps maintain DAI's peg tightly around $1.00.

stability_fee.definition: The interest rate charged on debt in MakerDAO Vaults. Set by MKR governance. Functions like an interest rate—users must pay this fee when repaying their DAI debt to unlock collateral.
